title: How does water climb to the top of a tall tree?
group: HOWN — How and Why in Nature

explain.say: A tall tree has no heart and no pump, yet it lifts hundreds of litres of water a day from its roots to leaves high above. The secret is that the water is pulled from the top, not pushed from the bottom.

faq.q: How do roots take in water?
faq.a: Roots are covered in thousands of tiny root hairs that give a huge surface touching the soil. Water moves into them because the root cells hold more dissolved substances than the soil water does.
Xylem is the plant's water pipework: long, hollow tubes made of dead cells joined end to end. In a tree the wood is mostly xylem, and the newest outer wood carries most of the water.
asks: What are the water pipes in a plant?

faq.a: Transpiration is water evaporating from a plant's leaves through its stomata. It cools the plant and pulls fresh water and minerals up from the roots.
asks: Why do plants lose water from their leaves?

faq.q: Why doesn't the water fall back down?
faq.a: Water molecules stick to each other and to the walls of the narrow xylem tubes. Those pulls hold the column together, so the water hangs like a chain from the leaves.
asks: How does water stay up in a tree?

faq.q: Is there a limit to how tall a tree can grow?
faq.a: Yes. Scientists think the pull needed to lift water becomes too great at around 120 to 130 metres, close to the height of the tallest trees alive today.
asks: Why can trees not grow taller?

facts: The US Geological Survey estimates a large oak tree can give off about 150,000 litres of water a year through its leaves.
A 2004 study of tall redwoods estimated the greatest possible tree height at about 122 to 130 metres.
Most of the water a plant takes in is lost by transpiration; only a small part is used in photosynthesis.

quiz.say: What mainly pulls water up to the top of a tree?
quiz.show: What mainly pulls water up to the top of a tree?
quiz.why: Water evaporating from the leaves tugs a continuous thread of water up through the xylem.

wrong.0: Trees have no pump; roots can push water only a little way.
wrong.2: Gravity pulls water down, not up.
